categories.name: Correlation versus causation
categories.learning_note: Two things changing together does not prove that one caused the other. Look for a fair comparison, a possible third factor, and evidence that can distinguish cause from coincidence.
topics: a causal claim without a comparison group
question_types: identify what evidence would support causation
separate a pattern from its explanation

categories.name: Statistical reasoning
categories.learning_note: Numbers need context. Ask how many people were counted, how they were selected, what the percentage is based on, and whether an average hides important differences.

categories.name: Source credibility
categories.learning_note: Trace a claim back to its original source. Check whether the source has relevant expertise and evidence, and whether independent reliable sources confirm it. Popularity alone is not proof.

categories.name: Logical fallacies
categories.learning_note: A logical fallacy is a mistake in how a conclusion is supported. Check whether the reasons actually connect to the claim; an attack on a person, for example, does not answer their evidence.
question_types: separate a claim from an attack on its speaker

categories.name: Emotional manipulation
categories.learning_note: Fear, anger, guilt, or urgency can pressure people to react quickly. Notice the emotion, pause, and check the evidence before believing or sharing.

categories.name: Alternative explanations
categories.learning_note: One event can have more than one possible explanation. Think of reasonable alternatives and ask what information would help tell them apart.

categories.name: AI-generated or manipulated media
categories.learning_note: A photo, video, or voice recording can be edited or generated. Appearance alone cannot prove it is genuine; look for the original context and independent ways to verify it.
